findings.finding: Insights: Tₐ·T_b square ⇔ Tₐ=d·r², T_b=d·s² with d square‑free. Then (2a+1)²−8d·r²=1, (2b+1)²−8d·s²=1 (Pell x²−8d·y²=1). For each d, solutions y₁<y₂<… give c=d·y_i·y_j (i<j). S(N)=∑_{d sf} d·∑_{i<j, d·y_i·y_j≤N} y_i y_j. Compute by enumerating Pell sequences per d up to bound N/d. Pitfall: many d (≈N^{2/3}) but most have large minimal y₁, limiting contributions. Use bound y₁·y₂≤N/d to prune d.

Insights: Tₙ = n(n+1)/2 ⇒ write Tₙ = d·u² where d is square‑free part. Any two indices with same d give solution: c = d·uᵢ·uⱼ. So S(N)=∑₍d₎ d·∑_{i<j, d·uᵢ·uⱼ≤N} uᵢuⱼ. Need all d‑classes of triangular numbers, list u’s, count unordered products ≤N/d. Use Pell‑type recurrences for each d (e.g., d=1 gives square‑triangular indices). Compute sums up to N=10³⁵ modulo 136101521. Pitfall: avoid double‑counting when same c arises from different (a,b). Ensure a<b ordering. Use fast enumeration via generating recurrences for each class.

Insights: a(a+1) and b(b+1) must share the same square‑free kernel K. Write a(a+1)=K·r², b(b+1)=K·s² ⇒ (2a+1)²−K(2r)²=1 (Pell). Solutions give sequences {r_i} for each square‑free K. Then c=√(T_aT_b)=(K/2)·r·s, with r≠s. For N, bound r·s≤2N/K. So S(N)=∑_{K sq‑free} (K/2)·∑_{i<j, r_i r_j≤⌊2N/K⌋} r_i r_j. Compute Pell sequences, enumerate pairs under bound, sum modulo 136101521. Pitfall: need only even y=2r solutions; ensure K includes factor 2 when odd (r even). Use fast Pell generation and two‑pointer counting for each K.

Insights: T_a·T_b square ⇔ sqf(T_a)=sqf(T_b)=d (square‑free). Write T_k=d·y² ⇒ (2k+1)²−8d·y²=1 (Pell X²−8dY²=1, X odd). For each square‑free d≠2, solutions (X_i,Y_i) give y_i. c=d·y_i·y_j, i<j.  

Goal: S(n)=∑_{d≠2} d·∑_{i<j, y_i y_j≤⌊n/d⌋} y_i y_j.  

Compute for each d: let N=⌊n/d⌋. Sequence y_i grows exponentially (Pell). Use double‑sum: Σ_{i<j, y_i y_j≤N} y_i y_j =½[∑_i y_i·S(N/y_i)−∑_{y_i²≤N} y_i²], where S(m)=∑_{y_j≤m} y_j.  

Since y_i≈α^i (α>1), only O(log N) terms per d. For large d, N<y₁² ⇒ contribution 0. Thus iterate d up to n/y₁² (≈n/(≈√d)²) → only O(√n) d? Actually y₁≈√(X₁−1)/2≈√(2d) so y₁≈√(2d). Hence condition N≥y₁² ⇒ n/d ≥2d ⇒ d≤√(n/2). So only d≤≈√n matter (~10¹⁷ for n=10³⁵). Still huge, but we can group d by same Pell fundamental solution? Use that y₁=√( (X₁−1)/2 )? Actually from X₁²−8dY₁²=1 minimal X₁ odd. For each d, X₁≈⌈√(8d)⌉+? Minimal solution often X₁=⌊√(8d)⌋+1. Approx y₁≈1.  

Key pitfall: d=2 gives D=16 square → no nontrivial solutions; exclude.  

Implementation: generate all square‑free d≤√(n/2). For each, solve Pell X²−8dY²=1 (fundamental solution via continued fraction). Generate y_i until y_i·y_{i+1}>N. Compute S(N) via prefix sums. Sum contributions modulo 136101521.

Insights: Tₙ·Tₘ is a square ⇔ Tₙ=d·u², Tₘ=d·v² with same square‑free d.  Pell: x²−8d y²=1 gives all (u,y).  Fundamental solution (x₁,y₁) ⇒ yₖ from yₖ₊₁=2x₁yₖ−yₖ₋₁.  Triples: c=d·u·v, c≤N.  Thus S(N)=∑_{d sf} d·∑_{i<j, uᵢuⱼ≤N/d} uᵢuⱼ.  Key: generate d with minimal u₁ small enough (c_min=2d·x₁·u₁²).  Pitfall: many d, but only those with c_min≤N matter; use Pell recurrences to list u’s and two‑pointer sum per d.  Compute modulo 136101521.

Insights: Tₙ = uₙ·vₙ with uₙ=n/gcd(n,2), vₙ=(n+1)/(2/gcd(n,2)). Write Tₙ = d·Y² where d is square‑free kernel. Then n solves n(n+1)/2 = d·Y² ⇔ (2n+1)²−8d·Y²=1, a Pell equation. For each square‑free d≠2·k² there are infinite solutions (Xₖ,Yₖ) from (X₁+Y₁√8d)ᵏ. Each pair (i<j) gives c = d·Yᵢ·Yⱼ. So S(N)=∑_{d} d·∑_{i<j, d·YᵢYⱼ≤N} YᵢYⱼ. Compute Y‑sequences via Pell recurrences, generate all (d,Yᵢ) with d·Y₁·Y₂≤N, sum contributions. Pitfall: d of form 2·k² yields no solutions; ensure Yᵢ integer (Yᵢ² = Tₙ/d). Use fast exponentiation for Pell powers; limit d by N/Y₁². This yields S(10³⁵) mod 136101521.

Insights: Tₐ·T_b square ⇔ Tₐ=d·r², T_b=d·s² with d square‑free. Then c=d·r·s and (2a+1)²−8d·r²=1, (2b+1)²−8d·s²=1 → Pell x²−8d·y²=1. For each square‑free triangular d=T_k (k s.t. T_k square‑free) the fundamental solution has y₁=1, x₁=2k+1. All y’s satisfy y_{n+1}=2x₁·y_n−y_{n−1}. Need S(N)=∑_{d square‑free triangular} d·∑_{i<j, d·y_i·y_j≤N} y_i·y_j. Use Pell recurrences to generate y’s per d; bound d·y₁·y₂≈2d·x₁≤N ⇒ d≤N^{2/3}. Compute contributions via two‑pointer per d. Verify S(10⁵),S(10⁹). Then evaluate S(10³⁵) mod 136101521. (Pitfall: ensure d square‑free; handle large N via efficient O(N^{2/3}) loops; use modular arithmetic.)

Insights: Tₐ·T_b square ⇔ Tₐ=d·u², T_b=d·v² with same square‑free d (d≠2).  a,b from Pell X²−8d·y²=1 (y=u,v).  c=d·u·v.  For each d, generate y‑sequence via (X₁+ y₁√D)ᵏ (D=8d).  Keep y≤⌊N/d⌋, compute Σ_{i<j}y_i y_j =((Σy)²−Σy²)/2, add d·that.  Only d with at least two y’s matter; roughly d≤N^{1/3}.  Compute all such d (square‑free, d≠2) up to N^{1/3}, get y‑lists via Pell recurrence, sum contributions mod 136101521. Insights: c²=TₐT_b ⇔ Tₐ=d·u², T_b=d·v² with d square‑free.  Then (2a+1)²–8d·u²=1, (2b+1)²–8d·v²=1 ⇒ (x,y) solve Pell x²–D·y²=1 with D=8d.  All solutions: yₖ from recurrence y₀=0, y₁=Y₁ (fundamental), yₖ₊₁=2X₁yₖ–yₖ₋₁.  For each d, c=d·y_i·y_j (i<j).  Need c≤N.  So S(N)=∑_{d sq‑free} d·∑_{i<j, y_i y_j≤N/d} y_i y_j.  Minimal c for d is c_min≈2√8·d^{3/2}·Y₁³; only d with c_min≤N matter (tiny).  For d triangular (d=T_n), Y₁=1, giving many solutions; other d have Y₁≥2, quickly exceed N.  Thus enumerate d up to ≈(N)^{2/3}, compute fundamental Pell (X₁,Y₁) via continued fractions, generate y‑sequence until d·y_i·y_{i+1}>N, sum pairs via two‑pointer.  This yields exact S(N) even for N=10³⁵ (few thousand d’s).  Pitfalls: ensure d square‑free, handle Y₁=1 case (triangular d) correctly, use 64‑bit/BigInt for N≈10³⁵, mod after each addition.

Insights: c²=TₐT_b ⇔ sqf(Tₐ)=sqf(T_b)=d (square‑free, d≠2). Write Tₐ=d·y₁², T_b=d·y₂² where (X,y) solves X²−8d·y²=1 (Pell). Then c=d·y₁y₂.  

Thus S(N)=∑_{d sq‑free≠2} d·∑_{i<j, y_i y_j≤N/d} y_i y_j, where {y_i} are Pell‑Y‑values for D=8d.  

Key: For each d, y_i grow exponentially (≈ε^i). Only O(log N) terms per d. Most d give no contribution; only d with small minimal y (often y₁=1 when 8d+1 is a square, i.e. d=T_k) matter.  

Pitfall: naïve loop over all d≤N impossible; must restrict to d with y₁·y₂≤N/d (≈d≤N^{2/3}) and use Pell recurrences. Use μ²(d) to test square‑free. Compute fundamental solution (X₁,Y₁) via continued fractions, generate y_i via (X+Y√D)ⁿ. Sum pairs with product bound.  

Result: implement fast enumeration of d up to N^{2/3} (≈10^{23.3} for N=10^{35})? Actually need analytic summation; further reduction using density of triangular d (≈√N) and bounding contributions yields O(N^{1/3}) terms, feasible with modular arithmetic.

Insights: Tₙ=d·u² ⇔ (2n+1)²−8d·u²=1 (Pell). For each square‑free d≠2, solutions (Xₖ,Yₖ) give nₖ=(Xₖ−1)/2, uₖ=Yₖ. Every triple (a,b,c) ↔ (d,i<j) with c=d·uᵢ·uⱼ. Thus S(N)=∑_{d sf≠2} d·∑_{i<j, uᵢuⱼ≤N/d} uᵢuⱼ. Need to generate all d,u‑sequences up to N≈10³⁵ efficiently. Pitfall: d runs to ~N^{2/3} (≈10²³) – cannot brute‑force. Must exploit that only d with small minimal u (often u=1 for triangular d) contribute many terms; others quickly exceed bound. Use Pell recurrences per d, prune when d·u₁·u₂>N. Compute contributions modulo 136101521.

Insights: T_a·T_b=c² ⇔ T_a=d·u², T_b=d·v² (d square‑free). Write a(a+1)=2d u² ⇒ (2a+1)²−8d u²=1 (Pell X²−8dY²=1). For each square‑free d (≠2) solutions Y_i give u_i; c=d·u_i·u_j (i<j). Minimal case d=T_k (triangular) has u₁=1, u₂=2(2k+1) ⇒ c_k=k(k+1)(2k+1). Sum of all such minima ≤N: K=floor(max k with k(k+1)(2k+1)≤N); Σc_k=K(K+1)²(K+2)/2. Other d give O((log N)²) terms each, negligible vs N^{4/3} but needed modulo M. Compute contributions per d via Y‑sequence (recurrence X_{n+1}=6X_n−X_{n−1}, Y_{n+1}=6Y_n−Y_{n−1}) up to √(N/d). Sum S(N)=∑_{d} d·[(ΣY)²−ΣY²]/2 mod M. Use binary search for K, fast recurrence for Y, and iterate d only while d·Y₁·Y₂≤N (≈N^{1/3} d’s). Compute all terms mod 136101521.

Insights: TₐT_b=c² ⇔ a(a+1)b(b+1)=4c². Write X=2a+1, Y=2b+1 ⇒ (X²−1)(Y²−1)=(8c)². Hence for each square‑free d≠2, solutions of X²−8d·u²=1 give Tₐ=d·u². For a fixed d, u‑values are Pell‑Y’s; c=d·u_i·u_j. Main contribution comes from d that are triangular numbers (d=T_n) with u₁=1, giving c_min=n(n+1)(2n+1). Condition T_n square‑free ⇔ n and n+1 odd‑square‑free and the even one has v₂≤2 (no factor 8). So S(N)≈∑_{n≤N^{1/3}, T_n sq‑free} n(n+1)(2n+1) plus small corrections from higher u’s. Compute this sum via Möbius: I(n)=[square‑free odd n][square‑free odd (n+1)]·[v₂(even)≤2]. Use μ(d) over odd squares: I(n)=∑_{d₁,d₂ odd}μ(d₁)μ(d₂)·[d₁²|n][d₂²|(n+1)]·cond₂. Then S(N)=∑_{d₁,d₂}μ(d₁)μ(d₂)∑_{k≤X/(lcm(d₁²,d₂²))} f(k) with f(k)=c_min evaluated at n satisfying congruences, handling parity (v₂≤2) via case split (n odd/even). Compute sums up to X≈N^{1/3} (≈5·10¹¹) using divisor‑sieving O(√X) ≈7·10⁵ loops, feasible. Add corrections from higher u‑pairs (few per d). Finally output S(10³⁵) mod 136101521. Pitfalls: ensure d≠2, handle v₂ condition correctly, avoid double‑counting, use 64‑bit/BigInt for intermediate sums before mod.

Insights: Tₐ·T_b square ⇔ Tₐ=d·r², T_b=d·s² with d square‑free (d=T_k for some k where T_k is square‑free). Then (2a+1)²–8d·r²=1, (2b+1)²–8d·s²=1 → Pell x²–8d·y²=1. For each square‑free triangular d, solutions y₁=1, y_{n+1}=2X·y_n–y_{n-1} (X=2k+1, k s.t. d=T_k). c=d·y_i·y_j, i<j, c≤N. Count triples via base index k (a₀) with d=T_{a₀}; condition for any pair: a₀³≈N ⇒ a₀≤N^{1/3}. Each k contributes O(log N) pairs (tiny for large k). Sum S(N)=∑_{k≤N^{1/3}} d·∑_{i<j, d·y_i·y_j≤N} y_i·y_j. Use recurrence to generate y_i per k, stop when product exceeds N/d. Compute modulo 136101521. Pitfall: ensure d square‑free (check μ²(d)=1). Use fast integer arithmetic; N=10³⁵ ⇒ k≈10^{11.7}, but only O(N^{1/3}) loops with tiny inner loops.

Insights: $c^2=T_aT_b\iff a(a+1)b(b+1)=(2c)^2$. Write $a(a+1)=d\,u^2$, $b(b+1)=d\,v^2$ with $d$ square‑free. Then $c=\frac d2uv$ and $u,v$ are $Y/2$ from Pell $X^2-dY^2=1$ with $X$ odd, $Y$ even.  

Thus for each square‑free $d$, let $U_d=\{u_i\}$ (increasing, $u_{i+1}\approx\lambda_d u_i$, $\lambda_d>1$).  

$S(N)=\sum_{d\ \text{sq‑free}}\frac d2\sum_{i<j,\;u_i u_j\le 2N/d}u_i u_j$.  

Key: $U_d$ grows exponentially, so for given $N$ only $u_i\le\sqrt{2N/d}$ needed → $O(\log N)$ terms per $d$.  

But many $d$ (pronic $d=m(m+1)$, $u_{\min}=1$) satisfy $d\le2N$, giving $≈\sqrt N$ such $d$ → impossible to enumerate.  

Thus need analytic summation over $d$ using density of square‑free pronic numbers and Pell growth; $S(N)\sim C\,N(\ln N)^5$.  

Pitfalls: assuming few $d$; ignoring parity of Pell solutions; missing $u_{\min}>1$ cases.
